title: Used Ferrari Roma for Sale in Miami: 2026 Pricing, Dealers & Buyer's Guide
excerpt: The Ferrari Roma is one of the most elegant grand tourers Ferrari has ever built — and used examples are finally hitting Miami's market at approachable prices. Here's what to look for, what to pay, and where to find one in South Florida.
content:
The Ferrari Roma arrived in 2020 as a deliberate departure from Ferrari's sharp-edged, aggressive design language. Inspired by the dolce vita spirit of 1960s Rome, it's a front-engined V8 grand tourer that prioritizes elegance over aggression — and in Miami, where the car scene skews loud and flashy, the Roma has become the thinking enthusiast's Ferrari.

Now, with the first wave of lease returns and trade-ins arriving at South Florida dealerships, used Ferrari Roma prices have dropped into genuinely compelling territory. Here's everything you need to know about buying a pre-owned Roma in Miami in 2026.

Used Ferrari Roma Pricing in Miami: What You'll Actually Pay

When the Roma launched, MSRP started around $222,620 — but most buyers specced theirs well north of $250,000 with options. The used market tells a different story:

Model YearMileage RangeMiami Market Pricevs. Original MSRP
202115,000–25,000 mi$195,000–$215,000-15% to -22%
20228,000–18,000 mi$210,000–$235,000-10% to -18%
20233,000–12,000 mi$225,000–$260,000-5% to -12%
2024 Roma SpiderUnder 5,000 mi$275,000–$310,000-3% to -8%

The sweet spot for most buyers is a 2022 model with under 15,000 miles — you're looking at roughly $215,000–$230,000, which gets you a relatively fresh car with all the modern tech and a seven-year manufacturer warranty that still has years remaining.

Why the Ferrari Roma Is Perfect for Miami

Miami's car culture tends to reward the loudest, widest, most attention-grabbing machines. The Roma takes the opposite approach — and that's exactly why it works here.

  • Grand touring comfort: Miami traffic is brutal. The Roma's 612-horsepower twin-turbo V8 paired with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission delivers effortless power without the kidney-punching ride of a 296 GTB or SF90.
  • Subtle presence: The Roma's flowing lines and minimalist design turn heads without screaming for attention. At a valet stand full of Huracáns, a Roma in Grigio Titanio or Blu Roma stands out by standing apart.
  • Convertible option: The Roma Spider (2023+) is a retractable hardtop — perfect for A1A cruises without the structural compromises of a soft-top.
  • Usable trunk: With 8.8 cubic feet of cargo space, the Roma can actually handle a weekend getaway to Key West or Naples.

Key Specs: Ferrari Roma at a Glance

SpecificationDetails
Engine3.9L twin-turbo V8
Horsepower612 hp @ 7,500 RPM
Torque561 lb-ft @ 3,000–5,750 RPM
Transmission8-speed dual-clutch automatic
0–60 mph3.3 seconds
Top Speed199 mph
Curb Weight3,461 lbs
LayoutFront-engine, rear-wheel drive
Seating2+2

Where to Find a Used Ferrari Roma in Miami

South Florida has more Ferrari inventory than almost anywhere else in the country. Here are the best places to start your search:

Ferrari of Miami (The Collection)

Located in Coral Gables, The Collection is Miami's authorized Ferrari dealer and typically has the largest selection of certified pre-owned Romas. CPO cars come with extended warranty coverage and a thorough multi-point inspection. Expect to pay a slight premium over independent dealers, but the peace of mind is worth it for a Ferrari.

Prestige Imports

On NW 36th Street, Prestige regularly stocks used Ferraris alongside their Lamborghini franchise. Their Roma inventory tends to be well-specced trade-ins from local collectors upgrading to the 296 GTB or 12Cilindri.

Curated Miami

This boutique dealer in Wynwood focuses on hand-picked exotic inventory. Their Romas tend to be lower-mileage, higher-spec examples — think carbon fiber options packages, racing seats, and rare paint colors.

RMC Miami

A trusted independent option on NW 36th Street. RMC stocks a rotating selection of Ferraris with transparent vehicle histories. Good place to find a deal, especially on examples with slightly higher mileage.

Online Marketplaces

Don't overlook DuPont Registry, Bring a Trailer, and Cars & Bids — all three regularly list Romas, and with Miami's massive exotic car market, you can often find local sellers willing to do a deal without cross-country shipping complications.

Used Ferrari Roma: What to Inspect Before Buying

The Roma is mechanically robust, but there are specific things to watch for on used examples:

  • Brake wear: Ferrari's carbon-ceramic brakes (optional) are effectively lifetime components. Standard steel brakes, however, wear faster in Miami's stop-and-go traffic. Budget $3,000–$5,000 for a front brake job on steel rotors.
  • Paint condition: Miami's UV exposure and salt air are brutal on dark-colored Ferraris. Check for clear coat fading, micro-scratches, and whether paint protection film (PPF) was applied from new.
  • Tire age vs. mileage: Low-mileage garage queens may have original tires that look good but have degraded rubber. Check the DOT date code — tires older than 4 years should be replaced regardless of tread depth.
  • Warranty status: Ferrari's standard warranty is 3 years/unlimited miles, with a 7-year maintenance program. Verify both are still active and transferable. Extended warranty programs through Ferrari are available and highly recommended.
  • Service history: Insist on full Ferrari dealer service records. Independent shop service isn't a dealbreaker, but it can affect resale value and CPO eligibility.

Insurance and Running Costs in Miami

Owning a Ferrari in Miami isn't just the purchase price. Here's what to budget annually:

Cost CategoryAnnual Estimate
Insurance (full coverage)$5,500–$9,000
Annual service (7-year program)Included if active
Annual service (out of program)$2,500–$4,000
Tires (set of 4)$1,800–$2,400
Registration & taxes (FL)$800–$1,200
Detailing & PPF maintenance$1,500–$3,000

Florida's lack of state income tax and relatively low registration fees make it one of the most affordable states to own an exotic car — which is one reason so many end up here.

Used Ferrari Roma vs. the Competition in Miami

At the $200K–$250K used price point, the Roma competes with some serious alternatives:

ModelUsed Price RangeBest For
Ferrari Roma$195K–$260KElegant GT cruising, brand prestige
Porsche 911 Turbo S (992)$190K–$230KAll-weather performance, daily driving
Aston Martin DB11 V8$140K–$180KBritish GT elegance, value proposition
McLaren GT$160K–$200KLong-distance comfort, unique design
Maserati MC20$185K–$230KItalian mid-engine exotic, Nettuno V6

The Roma holds its own on driving dynamics and absolutely dominates on badge cachet. In Miami, the prancing horse still carries weight that no other brand quite matches — and the Roma delivers it without the maintenance headaches of older Ferrari V8s.

Should You Buy a Used Ferrari Roma in Miami?

If you want a Ferrari that you can actually use — drive to dinner in South Beach, take down to the Keys for a weekend, park at the office without worrying about curb rash on a wide-body supercar — the Roma is the answer. It's the most livable Ferrari in the current lineup, and the used market has finally made it accessible to buyers who would've been priced out of a new one.

Miami's used exotic market is deep, competitive, and full of well-maintained examples. The key is patience: wait for the right spec, verify the service history, and negotiate — used Ferrari prices in Miami are more flexible than most people think, especially on units that have been sitting on a dealer lot for 60+ days.

The Ferrari Roma isn't the fastest, the loudest, or the most extreme Ferrari you can buy. It's the one you'll actually enjoy owning every day. And in a city where your car is an extension of your lifestyle, that counts for a lot.

title: Brabus G-Wagon for Sale in Miami: 2026 Pricing, Models & Where to Find One
excerpt: From the 700 Widestar to the 900 Rocket, Brabus-tuned Mercedes G-Class SUVs have become Miami status symbols. Here's your complete guide to buying a Brabus G-Wagon in South Florida — pricing, models, dealers, and what to watch for.
content:
The Mercedes-AMG G 63 already dominates Miami's streets like no other vehicle. But for a certain tier of buyer, the standard G-Wagon isn't enough. Enter Brabus — the German tuning house that takes Mercedes' iconic military-bred SUV and transforms it into something genuinely absurd: wider, louder, more powerful, and finished to a level that makes the stock G 63 feel restrained.

If you've been searching for a Brabus G-Wagon for sale in Miami, you're not alone. Demand in South Florida has surged over the past two years, and the market for both new builds and pre-owned Brabus G-Class models is more active than ever. Here's everything you need to know before writing that check.

Brabus G-Wagon Models & Pricing in Miami

Brabus offers multiple tiers of G-Class modification, from subtle power upgrades to full ground-up builds. Here's what each level looks like in the current Miami market:

ModelHorsepowerBase Price (New Build)Used Market (Miami)Key Features
Brabus 700700 hp$350,000–$400,000$280,000–$350,000Power upgrade, Brabus exhaust, interior trim
Brabus 800800 hp$450,000–$550,000$380,000–$480,000800 hp, Widestar body kit, forged wheels
Brabus 900900 hp$600,000–$750,000$500,000–$650,0004.5L destroked V8, full aero, extreme interior
Brabus 900 Rocket Edition900 hp$800,000+$700,000–$900,000+Limited to 25 units, carbon widebody, bespoke everything
Brabus 800 Adventure XLP800 hp$500,000–$600,000$420,000–$550,000Pickup truck conversion, portal axles, off-road kit

Prices vary significantly based on spec, condition, and how many factory options were added to the base G 63 before the Brabus conversion. A fully loaded Brabus 800 Widestar with a bespoke interior can easily exceed $600,000 — while a tastefully modified Brabus 700 with modest options might come in under $300,000 used.

Why Brabus G-Wagons Dominate Miami

It's not a coincidence that Miami has become the unofficial Brabus G-Wagon capital of America. The convergence of factors is almost too perfect:

  • Visibility culture: Miami rewards vehicles that make a statement. A Brabus Widestar, with its flared fenders, massive wheels, and aggressive exhaust note, delivers that on a level the stock G 63 can't match.
  • Flat terrain: The G-Wagon's truck-like ride quality matters less when you're cruising flat coastal roads versus mountain passes. Miami's geography is actually ideal for these heavy, high-riding SUVs.
  • Valet-friendly: Unlike a low-slung supercar, a Brabus G-Wagon handles parking garages, speed bumps, and valet situations without drama. It's the only $500K+ vehicle you can daily drive without constant anxiety about scraping.
  • Celebrity and influencer effect: When every other high-profile Miami resident — athletes, musicians, tech founders — is driving a modified G-Wagon, the aspirational demand follows. Brabus sits at the top of that food chain.
  • Resale strength: Brabus G-Wagons hold value remarkably well. The limited-production models (Rocket Edition, certain XLP builds) have actually appreciated since delivery.

Where to Buy a Brabus G-Wagon in Miami

Finding an authentic Brabus build requires some diligence — the market is full of aftermarket G-Wagon body kits and cosmetic clones that claim to be "Brabus-style" but aren't genuine. Here's where to shop for the real thing:

Brabus Miami (Authorized Dealer)

Brabus has an authorized presence in South Florida through select dealer partners. An authorized source guarantees genuine Brabus parts, proper ECU tuning, and a transferable Brabus warranty that supplements the Mercedes factory coverage. This is the safest route for a new build — you spec a G 63 through Mercedes, and Brabus handles the conversion.

The Collection (Coral Gables)

As Mercedes-Benz's premier South Florida dealer, The Collection occasionally stocks Brabus-modified G-Class units as pre-owned inventory. Their service department is equipped to handle Brabus-specific maintenance, which is a significant advantage for long-term ownership.

Prestige Imports

Prestige regularly lists Brabus G-Wagons alongside their Lamborghini and Bentley inventory. They tend to carry higher-spec builds — Brabus 800 and above — and their units are typically consignment vehicles from local collectors.

Curated Miami / RMC Miami

Both boutique dealers have handled Brabus G-Class inventory. Expect hand-picked examples with full documentation. Curated in particular focuses on unique specs that stand out even among other Brabus builds.

Online & Auction

DuPont Registry is ground zero for high-end Brabus listings nationally. Bring a Trailer has started to see more Brabus G-Wagons as well, though the truly limited models tend to sell through private brokers rather than public auctions.

Brabus G-Wagon: What Makes It Different from a Stock G 63

The question everyone asks: is a Brabus really worth 2-3x the price of a standard G 63? Here's what you're actually getting:

Powertrain

The stock G 63 makes 577 hp from its 4.0L twin-turbo V8. Brabus extracts up to 900 hp from the same engine block through larger turbochargers, upgraded intercoolers, a proprietary ECU tune, and a high-performance exhaust system. The Brabus 900 actually uses a bored-and-stroked 4.5L version of the V8 — it's essentially a new engine.

Exterior

The Widestar body kit adds flared wheel arches, an aggressive front bumper with integrated LED lighting, carbon fiber hood scoops, a roof-mounted light bar, and Brabus Monoblock forged wheels (up to 24 inches). The overall effect makes the G-Wagon look 30% more aggressive while maintaining OEM-level fit and finish.

Interior

This is where Brabus truly justifies the premium. Full leather or Alcantara retrim in virtually any color combination. Carbon fiber or forged carbon trim. Illuminated Brabus logos. Starlight headliner. Custom stitching patterns. Floor mats that cost more than most people's car payments. The interior quality genuinely rivals Rolls-Royce.

Exhaust

The Brabus valve-controlled exhaust system is the single most transformative upgrade. In comfort mode, it's barely louder than stock. In sport mode, it produces a baritone V8 roar that echoes off the buildings on Ocean Drive. It's the audio equivalent of the Brabus visual transformation.

Brabus G-Wagon Insurance in Miami

Insuring a Brabus G-Wagon in Miami requires specialty coverage. Here's what to expect:

Coverage TypeAnnual Cost Estimate
Full coverage (Brabus 700)$8,000–$12,000
Full coverage (Brabus 800/900)$12,000–$20,000
Agreed value policy15–25% more than standard
Comprehensive only (garaged/limited use)$3,000–$6,000

Critical tip: Standard auto insurance policies will only cover the base G 63 value, not the Brabus modifications. You need an agreed-value policy from a specialty insurer like Hagerty, Chubb, or PURE that covers the full modified value. Without this, a total loss claim could leave you $200,000+ short.

Used Brabus G-Wagon: What to Inspect

Buying a pre-owned Brabus build requires extra due diligence beyond a standard used car inspection:

  • Verify Brabus authenticity: Every genuine Brabus build comes with a Brabus certificate of authenticity and a unique build number. Ask for this documentation. If the seller can't produce it, walk away — you're likely looking at aftermarket parts installed by a third-party shop.
  • ECU tune verification: The Brabus ECU tune should be logged and verifiable. Brabus Miami or an authorized dealer can confirm whether the tune is genuine and hasn't been further modified by a local shop.
  • Wheel and tire condition: Brabus Monoblock wheels are forged aluminum and expensive to replace ($2,000–$4,000 per wheel). Check for curb rash, cracks, and proper tire sizing. Miami's potholes and parking garage ramps are tough on large-diameter wheels.
  • Suspension and alignment: Modified G-Wagons with lowered suspension (some Brabus packages include this) are more susceptible to alignment issues on Miami's uneven roads. Get a four-corner alignment check before buying.
  • Service records: Brabus recommends service at authorized facilities. Verify that the vehicle has been maintained on schedule and that any Brabus-specific components (exhaust valves, turbo systems, intercoolers) have been inspected.
  • Interior wear: Brabus interiors use premium materials that require proper care. Check leather and Alcantara surfaces for UV fading (common in Miami), dye transfer from clothing, and wear on high-touch surfaces like the steering wheel and center console.

Running Costs: What to Budget Annually

CategoryAnnual Estimate
Insurance (agreed value)$10,000–$20,000
Scheduled maintenance$3,000–$5,000
Tires (set of 4, 23" or 24")$2,500–$4,000
Fuel (premium, ~12 MPG city)$5,000–$7,000
Detailing & PPF$2,000–$4,000
Registration (FL)$800–$1,500

Total annual running cost for a Brabus G-Wagon in Miami: $23,000–$41,000 depending on the model tier and how much you drive. This isn't a frugal vehicle — but buyers at this level aren't optimizing for cost-per-mile.

Brabus G-Wagon vs. Other Modified G-Class Builds

Brabus isn't the only shop modifying G-Wagons. Here's how the major players compare:

BuilderPrice Premium over G 63Max HPMiami Availability
Brabus$100K–$500K+900 hpStrong (authorized dealer network)
Mansory$80K–$300K850 hpModerate (select dealers)
Lumma Design$30K–$80K700 hpLimited (online/import)
Hofele Design$40K–$120KStockLimited (cosmetic focus)
Local Miami shops$15K–$60KVariesHigh (but quality varies wildly)

Brabus commands the highest premium but also delivers the most comprehensive transformation, the best resale value, and the strongest warranty support. For Miami buyers planning to keep the vehicle more than 2-3 years, the Brabus premium pays for itself in retained value.

Should You Buy a Brabus G-Wagon in Miami?

The Brabus G-Wagon is the ultimate Miami vehicle. It's tall enough to see over traffic, powerful enough to merge onto I-95 with authority, luxurious enough for date night at Carbone, and imposing enough to justify its price tag every time you hand the keys to a valet. It handles the practical realities of Miami — rain, parking structures, rough roads — while delivering a level of exclusivity and presence that even a $300K supercar can't match.

The used market has created a real window of opportunity. A well-maintained Brabus 700 at $280,000–$320,000 offers an entry point into the Brabus world that would've been impossible three years ago. For the serious buyer, a pre-owned Brabus 800 Widestar in the $400K range represents the sweet spot: enough presence to stand out in a city full of G-Wagons, with running costs that are manageable for the target demographic.

Just make sure you're buying an authentic build with documentation, get an agreed-value insurance policy before you drive it off the lot, and budget for those 24-inch tire replacements. Welcome to the top of the G-Wagon food chain.

title: Best Convertibles for Miami in 2026: The Ultimate Drop-Top Living Guide
excerpt: From Porsche 911 Cabriolets cruising Ocean Drive to Mazda Miatas hugging the curves of Key Biscayne, here are the best convertibles to own in Miami right now — at every budget.
content:
Miami was made for convertibles. Twelve months of warm weather, palm-lined boulevards, ocean views from practically every highway — there's no city in America where going topless (the car, relax) makes more sense. But picking the right drop-top for South Florida life means thinking about more than just looks. You need something that handles heat, humidity, salt air, and the occasional five-minute monsoon that rolls through at 3 PM.

We broke down the best convertibles to own in Miami right now across every price range, from daily-driver affordable to "I just docked my yacht" extravagant.

What Makes a Great Miami Convertible?

Before we get into picks, here's what actually matters when you're dropping the top in the 305:

  • Fast-operating top: Miami rain appears from nowhere. You need a top that goes up in under 15 seconds — ideally while rolling at low speed.
  • Good A/C: Non-negotiable. You'll be top-up in traffic plenty. A weak A/C in a convertible in August will make you question every life choice.
  • UV-resistant interior: Miami sun destroys cheap leather. Look for ventilated seats and quality materials.
  • Trunk space: Convertible tops eat cargo room. If you need to haul anything beyond sunglasses and a gym bag, check trunk capacity carefully.
  • Salt-air durability: Coastal living corrodes everything. Aluminum construction and good undercoating matter.

Best Convertibles Under 0K

CarStarting MSRPTop SpeedWhy It Works in Miami
Mazda MX-5 Miata RF~0,000135 mphRetractable fastback, lightweight, insanely fun on A1A
Ford Mustang Convertible (EcoBoost)~5,000145 mphClassic American muscle look, decent trunk, great sound system
MINI Cooper Convertible~3,000130 mphPerfect for South Beach parking, quick top operation, personality for days

The Miata RF is the enthusiast's pick. That retractable hardtop means you're not worrying about a fabric top degrading in the sun, and the targa-style opening is quick enough for those surprise downpours. It's also small enough to actually find parking in Brickell.

The Mustang EcoBoost convertible gives you the look — and in Miami, the look matters. Cruising down Collins Avenue with the top down in a Mustang just hits different. The four-cylinder turbo won't win any drag races, but it's perfectly adequate and way better on gas than the GT.

Best Convertibles 0K–0K

CarStarting MSRPTop SpeedWhy It Works in Miami
BMW 4 Series Convertible (430i)~6,000155 mphHardtop convertible, premium interior, solid tech
Chevrolet Corvette Convertible (C8)~8,000194 mphMid-engine supercar looks at a fraction of the price. Miami icon.
Ford Mustang GT Convertible~8,000155 mphV8 rumble, aggressive styling, huge aftermarket support
Mercedes-Benz CLE Cabriolet~5,000149 mphElegant, quiet, retractable soft top with acoustic insulation

The C8 Corvette convertible is the undisputed champion of this bracket. It looks like it costs twice what it does, the hardtop retracts in 16 seconds, and the mid-engine layout gives it legitimate supercar proportions. There's a reason you can't drive two blocks in Brickell without seeing one. It's the best performance-per-dollar convertible in America, and in Miami's image-conscious scene, it punches way above its price.

The BMW 430i is for the person who wants refinement over rawness. The hardtop means zero top-related anxiety in the rain, and BMW's interior quality in this generation is genuinely excellent. It's the convertible you'd pick for a client dinner drive to Bal Harbour.

Best Luxury Convertibles 0K–50K

CarStarting MSRPTop SpeedWhy It Works in Miami
Porsche 911 Carrera Cabriolet~25,000183 mphThe benchmark. Timeless design, daily-drivable, holds value like gold.
BMW M4 Convertible~8,000155 mphTrack-capable with the top down. Aggressive but livable.
Maserati GranCabrio~40,000177 mphItalian drama, that V6 Nettuno sound, turns every head on Ocean Drive

If you're spending six figures on a convertible in Miami, the Porsche 911 Cabriolet is the answer to almost every question. It's fast enough to thrill, comfortable enough to daily, and holds its value better than almost any other sports car on the market. The 992-generation design looks timeless, and Porsche's engineering means it'll handle Miami's heat and humidity without drama for years. This is the car you see parked outside every high-end restaurant in Coral Gables for a reason.

Best Ultra-Luxury & Exotic Convertibles (50K+)

CarStarting MSRPTop SpeedWhy It Works in Miami
Ferrari Roma Spider~70,000199 mphArguably the most beautiful car on sale. Retractable hardtop.
Lamborghini Huracán Evo Spyder~60,000202 mphScreaming V10, maximum attention, Miami's signature exotic
Rolls-Royce Dawn~70,000155 mphThe ultimate grand touring convertible. Silence and luxury at any speed.
McLaren Artura Spider~60,000205 mphHybrid V6, lightweight, next-gen supercar tech
Bentley Continental GT Speed Convertible~10,000208 mphW12 power with handcrafted interior. Star Island energy.

At this level, you're not buying transportation — you're buying an experience and a statement. The Ferrari Roma Spider is our pick for the most "Miami" exotic convertible right now. It's got the prancing horse badge, obviously, but the Roma's design is more elegant and less aggressive than a 296 or SF90, which means it fits everywhere from a Design District gallery opening to a casual lunch in Coconut Grove.

The Rolls-Royce Dawn is in a class by itself. If your thing is quiet luxury — gliding down the MacArthur Causeway at sunset with barely a whisper from the twin-turbo V12 — nothing else comes close. It's also the best convertible for Miami's social scene: the rear seats are actually usable, and the interior makes every passenger feel like royalty.

Best Used Convertibles for Miami Under 5K

Not everyone's buying new, and Miami's used market is full of gems. Here are the best used drop-tops to hunt for:

CarUsed Price RangeYears to TargetWatch Out For
Porsche Boxster (981/982)8K–5K2013–2016IMS bearing (early models), check service records
BMW Z4 (E89)5K–2K2012–2016Hardtop mechanism issues, check if it operates smoothly
Mazda MX-5 (ND)8K–4K2016–2019Nearly bulletproof. Check for salt corrosion underneath.
Chevrolet Camaro Convertible6K–3K2016–2019Visibility is poor. Make sure top seals are intact.

The 981 Boxster is the steal of the decade. You get a mid-engine Porsche with a flat-six soundtrack for under 5K. In Miami, where the badge on your car matters (let's be honest), pulling up in a Porsche for well under the price of a new Camry is a cheat code.

Convertible Care Tips for Miami Owners

Owning a convertible here comes with a few extra responsibilities:

  • Ceramic coat the interior: UV protection for leather and plastic surfaces is essential when the top is down 300 days a year.
  • Never leave the top down overnight: Even if it's not going to rain. Morning dew + salt air = mildew on soft tops.
  • Invest in a windscreen: For two-seaters especially, a wind deflector turns highway cruising from "shouting over wind" to actually enjoyable.
  • Keep an emergency top kit: Extra fuses, a manual override guide for electronic tops, and a rain cover in the trunk. Miami weather is unpredictable.
  • Park in shade or use a UV-blocking windshield cover: Interior temps in a parked convertible can exceed 170°F in direct Miami sun.

The Bottom Line

There's no wrong convertible in Miami — but there are better ones. If you want the best all-around Miami drop-top experience, the C8 Corvette Convertible wins on value, the Porsche 911 Cabriolet wins on everything else, and the Miata wins on pure driving joy per dollar. Whatever you choose, get the top down tonight and take A1A from South Beach to Sunny Isles. That's what living in Miami is for.

title: Miami's Worst Speed Traps and Traffic Cameras: Where You'll Get Caught in 2026
excerpt: From the I-95 express lanes to sneaky school zones in Coral Gables, here's where Miami drivers are getting hit with the most tickets — and how to protect your wallet.
content:
If you drive in Miami, you've either gotten a ticket, narrowly avoided one, or you're lying. Between aggressive red-light cameras, school-zone speed traps that appear out of nowhere, and enforcement zones on highways that seem designed to catch you mid-lane-change, Miami-Dade County is one of the most ticket-heavy metro areas in the entire United States.

We mapped out the spots where Miami drivers are getting caught the most in 2026 — and what you can actually do about it.

Miami's Red-Light Camera Hotspots

Florida is one of the states that still allows red-light cameras, and Miami-Dade has leaned into them hard. The county operates one of the largest red-light camera programs in the state, generating tens of millions in revenue annually.

IntersectionAreaWhy It's Brutal
NW 27th Ave & NW 79th StLiberty CityHigh volume, short yellow light timing, heavy enforcement
Biscayne Blvd & NE 163rd StNorth Miami BeachRight-turn-on-red violations — cameras catch incomplete stops
SW 8th St (Calle Ocho) & SW 87th AveWestchesterBusy commercial corridor, lots of lane weaving triggers
US-1 & SW 152nd StSouth Miami-DadeTricky light timing coming off highway speed
NW 36th St & NW 72nd AveDoralNear MIA airport — confused drivers plus aggressive cabbies

The fine: Red-light camera tickets in Miami-Dade are 58 for a first offense. They don't add points to your license (it's treated as a civil infraction, like a parking ticket), but they absolutely add up if you're a repeat offender. And if you ignore them, they go to collections.

Highway Speed Enforcement Zones

Miami's highways are where the real money gets made. Here are the stretches where FHP (Florida Highway Patrol) and local police camp out consistently:

HighwaySectionSpeed LimitEnforcement Style
I-95 SouthboundGolden Glades to I-195 merge55 mphFHP cruisers parked on shoulder, laser speed guns
I-95 Express LanesFull corridor55 mphSunPass data + patrol. Lanes feel fast, limit doesn't change.
Palmetto Expressway (SR-826)NW 36th St to Bird Rd55 mphMiami-Dade police love the median openings here
Dolphin Expressway (SR-836)Westbound near 57th Ave55 mphConstruction zones with doubled fines, frequently monitored
Florida TurnpikeHomestead Extension (south of SW 152nd)65 mphWide open road encourages speeding. FHP knows it.

The I-95 express lanes are the single biggest trap for Miami drivers. The lanes feel like they should be 70+ mph — they're smooth, elevated, and separated from general traffic. But the limit is 55, and FHP patrols them heavily. Doing 75 in the express lanes is practically normal flow, but it's also 20 over the limit, which is a 81 fine and 4 points on your license.

School Zone Speed Traps

This is where Miami gets truly ruthless. School zone speed limits drop to 15 mph during posted hours, and the fines for violations are doubled. Some of the most notorious school zone traps:

LocationSchoolWhy It's a Trap
Coral Way near SW 32nd AveCoral Gables PreparatorySpeed drops from 35 to 15 with minimal warning on a fast-flowing road
Brickell Ave near SE 12th StSouthside ElementaryMajor commuter corridor, easy to miss the zone change
Bird Road near SW 67th AveMultiple schoolsExtended school zone with camera enforcement
NE 2nd Ave in Design DistrictJose de Diego MiddleGentrified area, lots of distracted drivers, active enforcement

The math hurts: A school zone speeding ticket in Florida starts at 0 for 1–5 mph over (doubled to 00), but jumps to 50+ for 15 mph over, plus mandatory court appearance for 30+ over. Combined with the 15 mph limit, even going 35 in a school zone puts you 20 over — that's a 00 fine and 4 points.

Sneaky Municipal Speed Traps

Several small municipalities in the Miami metro have become notorious for aggressive speed enforcement that critics call revenue-driven:

  • Miami Gardens: Once issued more red-light camera tickets than any city in America. The program was scaled back after public backlash but still operates.
  • Virginia Gardens: Tiny town next to MIA airport. NW 36th Street goes through it, and they enforce aggressively on a stretch most drivers don't realize has a 30 mph limit.
  • Medley: Industrial area along NW 74th Street and Okeechobee Road. Trucks and commuters get tagged for going with traffic flow, which exceeds posted limits.
  • Sweetwater: Known for speed traps on 8th Street (Tamiami Trail). Limit drops in spots and local police patrol actively.
  • Bal Harbour: Collins Avenue enforcement. Tourists in rental convertibles are easy targets going 40 in a 30.

How to Protect Yourself

You can't drive in Miami without some risk, but here are practical steps to minimize your ticket exposure:

1. Use Waze Religiously

Waze's community-reported speed traps and police alerts are the single most effective tool Miami drivers have. The app's data in South Florida is incredibly accurate because the user base is massive. Set it as your default navigation even on routes you know by heart.

2. Know the Fine Structure

MPH Over LimitFine (Regular Zone)Fine (School/Construction)Points
1–5 mph29583
6–9 mph04083
10–14 mph54083
15–19 mph79584
20–29 mph04084
30+ mph79+58+4 + mandatory court

3. Consider a Quality Radar Detector

Florida is one of the states where radar detectors are fully legal. A quality unit like the Valentine One Gen2 or Uniden R8 will alert you to laser and radar enforcement. Not foolproof — instant-on laser is hard to detect — but they add a layer of awareness.

4. Fight Red-Light Camera Tickets

You have the right to contest red-light camera tickets. Common defenses include: the yellow light duration was below the legal minimum (3 seconds in Florida), you were already past the stop line when the light turned red, or the camera was improperly calibrated. A traffic attorney consultation for camera tickets typically costs less than the ticket itself.

5. Take Traffic School

Florida allows you to elect traffic school once per year (every 12 months) to avoid points from a speeding ticket. It costs around 5–0 for an online course and keeps your insurance from spiking. If you drive in Miami regularly, you should consider this a renewable annual resource — because you'll probably need it.

The Real Talk

Miami's traffic enforcement is a revenue machine — that's not cynical, it's documented. Miami-Dade County's red-light camera program alone generates over 0 million annually. But that doesn't mean you can't drive smart. Know the hotspots, use Waze, slow down through school zones (seriously, there are kids), and save the spirited driving for track days at Homestead-Miami Speedway. Your wallet — and your insurance rate — will thank you.

title: April 2026 in Miami: The Car Events, Auctions & Rallies You Need on Your Calendar
excerpt: From supercar rallies through Brickell to exclusive auctions in Coral Gables, April is stacked with automotive events across South Florida. Here's your complete guide to what's happening this month.
content:
April in Miami means one thing for car enthusiasts: the calendar is absolutely packed. As snowbirds make their last stand and the weather locks into that perfect 82°F sweet spot before summer humidity takes over, South Florida's automotive scene goes into overdrive. Here's every event worth your time this month.

Weekly Cars & Coffee Meetups

The backbone of Miami's car scene never stops. These weekly gatherings are free, casual, and consistently draw everything from barn-find muscle cars to fresh-off-the-truck McLarens.

EventLocationDay & TimeVibe
Cars & Coffee Palm BeachPalm Beach Outlets, West PalmSundays, 7–10 AM400+ cars, the big one
Supercar Saturdays FloridaRotates (Aventura, Boca, Ft. Lauderdale)Saturdays, 8–11 AMHeavy exotic presence
Brickell Cars & CoffeeBrickell City Centre garage rooftop1st & 3rd Saturdays, 8 AMUrban rooftop setting, great skyline backdrop
Miami Cars & CultureWynwood Art DistrictLast Saturday, 9 AMArt meets automotive, modified JDM welcome

The Gold Rush Rally Pit Stop — April 5–6

The legendary cross-country supercar rally makes its annual Miami pit stop, and it's always a spectacle. Expect 100+ exotic and hypercar entries rolling through Brickell and South Beach, with a public display event at Bayfront Park. Past years have seen Bugatti Chirons, Koenigseggs, and million-dollar one-offs parked casually along Biscayne Boulevard. Free to spectate — just show up.

RM Sotheby's Fort Lauderdale Auction — April 11–12

RM Sotheby's kicks off their spring Florida auction at the Broward County Convention Center. The consignment list is already stacking up with some notable lots:

  • 1973 Porsche 911 Carrera RS 2.7 — matching numbers, estimated $1.2–1.5M
  • 2024 Ferrari 296 GTS — under 500 miles, Assetto Fiorano package
  • 1967 Chevrolet Corvette 427/435 — frame-off restoration, NCRS Top Flight
  • 2023 Lamborghini Huracán Sterrato — one of the first in the US market

Preview is free and open to the public. Bidder registration runs $200. Even if you're not buying, walking the preview floor is worth it — these collections don't usually leave their climate-controlled garages.

Miami Auto Festival at Homestead-Miami Speedway — April 18–20

Three days of track time, car shows, and vendor exhibits at Homestead-Miami Speedway. The festival includes open lapping sessions (helmet and tech inspection required), a concours-style judged show, and a dedicated drift exhibition. Registration for track time starts at $350 for the weekend. Spectator passes are $25.

This year's featured marque is Porsche, with a dedicated display area for air-cooled 911s and a parade lap for the 50th anniversary of the 930 Turbo (yes, it's been half a century since the widowmaker debuted).

Wynwood Wheels Art & Auto Exhibition — April 25

Where Wynwood's street art culture meets automotive design. Local artists paint live on donor vehicles, custom builders show off their latest projects, and DJ sets keep the energy going into the evening. It's less about horsepower and more about aesthetics — think widebody builds with custom liveries, VIP-style Lexus sedans on air suspension, and art cars that blur the line between gallery and garage.

The event takes over 2nd Avenue between NW 23rd and 26th Streets. Free entry, though VIP packages ($75) get you access to the rooftop lounge with open bar.

Coral Gables Classic Car Cruise-In — Every Thursday in April

Miracle Mile shuts down to traffic every Thursday evening in April for the spring cruise-in series. Classic American iron dominates — Tri-Five Chevys, first-gen Mustangs, and big-block Mopars are the regulars. Cuban coffee from Versailles and a cruise down the mile is about as Miami as it gets.

What to Know Before You Go

TipDetails
Arrive earlyThe best cars at Cars & Coffee are gone by 9:30 AM. Serious enthusiasts show up at dawn.
Sunscreen is mandatoryApril sun in Miami is no joke — 85°F+ with UV index regularly hitting 10+.
Parking strategyFor Wynwood/Brickell events, rideshare in. Street parking fills fast and garages charge event pricing.
Camera gearPolarizing filters are your best friend for shooting cars in Florida sun. Cuts reflections, deepens paint colors.
Stay hydratedOutdoor events in April can feel like summer. Bring water — dehydration sneaks up fast.

April in Miami isn't just another month — it's the last window of perfect weather before the summer rain cycle starts in May. If you've been meaning to get out to more car events, this is the month to do it. See you out there.

title: Why Miami Is Becoming the #1 Destination for JDM Import Cars in 2026
excerpt: From R34 Skylines in Wynwood to Supras on Ocean Drive, Japanese Domestic Market imports are flooding South Florida. Here's what's driving the boom and where to find the best JDM dealers in Miami.
content:
Something shifted in Miami's car culture over the past two years, and it's impossible to ignore. Between the chrome Lamborghinis and lifted pickup trucks, a new category of car is turning heads on South Florida streets: Japanese Domestic Market imports. We're talking right-hand-drive Nissan Skyline GT-Rs, kei trucks delivering coffee in Wynwood, and pristine Toyota Supras with Japanese auction stickers still on the windshield.

Miami has quietly become the biggest JDM import hub on the East Coast — and 2026 is the year it went mainstream.

The 25-Year Rule Is Unlocking a Golden Era

The US federal government prohibits importing vehicles less than 25 years old that weren't originally sold here. That means 2026 is the magic year for cars built in 2001 — and the 2001 model year is absolutely stacked with JDM legends:

Now Legal in 2026Why It MattersEstimated Miami Market Price
Nissan Skyline R34 GT-R V-Spec IIThe holy grail. Peak GT-R before the R35 era.$180,000–$350,000
Nissan Silvia S15 Spec-RThe drift king. SR20DET turbo, gorgeous lines.$45,000–$75,000
Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution VIIRally-bred AWD turbo sedan, peak Evo.$40,000–$65,000
Honda Integra Type R (DC5)VTEC perfection, K20A engine.$35,000–$55,000
Subaru Impreza WRX STI (GDB)Bugeye STI, the one that started it all in the US.$30,000–$50,000
Suzuki Jimny (JB23)Tiny off-roader with cult following.$18,000–$28,000

Every year unlocks a new wave, but 2001 is special. These are the cars an entire generation grew up watching in Initial D, The Fast and the Furious, and Gran Turismo. Now they're old enough to legally import — and the buyers have the money.

Why Miami Specifically?

Port Miami and Port Everglades handle a combined 1 million+ TEUs of cargo annually, and the infrastructure for vehicle imports is well-established. But logistics alone don't explain the JDM boom. Here's what does:

  • No state income tax. Florida's tax-friendly environment attracts high-income collectors who'd rather spend on cars than send checks to Sacramento or Albany.
  • Year-round driving weather. JDM cars aren't garage queens here — owners actually drive them. No salt, no snow, no reason to hibernate a Skyline for six months.
  • No annual state inspection. Florida doesn't require vehicle inspections, which makes registering imported right-hand-drive vehicles significantly easier than in states with strict inspection regimes.
  • The culture. Miami already celebrates flashy, distinctive cars. A widebody S15 in midnight purple fits right in next to a Liberty Walk Ferrari. The city's DNA is showing off on wheels.
  • Latin American connection. Miami's role as a gateway to Latin America means established shipping routes and a multilingual dealer network comfortable with international transactions.

Where to Buy JDM in Miami

The JDM dealer scene in South Florida has exploded. Here are the shops that serious buyers are watching:

DealerLocationSpecialtyPrice Range
Toprank ImportersCypress Creek, Ft. LauderdaleFull-service JDM import, auction buying agent$25K–$300K+
JDM Expo FloridaDoralHigh-volume importer, 50+ cars in stock$20K–$150K
Rising Sun ImportsHialeahSkylines and GT-Rs specialist$60K–$400K
Pacific Coast AutoPompano BeachKei trucks and vans, Suzuki Carry specialist$8K–$25K
Duncan Imports & ClassicsOnline (ships to Miami)Largest US JDM inventory, 200+ vehicles$10K–$200K

Pro tip: If you want to buy directly from Japanese auctions, several Miami-based brokers will handle the entire process — bidding, shipping, customs clearance, EPA/DOT compliance, and Florida registration. Expect to pay $3,000–$5,000 in broker and shipping fees on top of the car's auction price.

The Kei Truck Phenomenon

It's not all six-figure GT-Rs. One of the most unexpected trends in Miami's JDM scene is the kei truck invasion. These tiny Japanese utility vehicles — Honda Acty, Suzuki Carry, Daihatsu Hijet — are showing up everywhere: food trucks in Wynwood, landscaping rigs in Coral Gables, and quirky daily drivers in Coconut Grove.

At $8,000–$15,000 for a clean example, they're accessible. Florida's lack of inspection requirements means registration is straightforward. And in a city where parking is a blood sport, a vehicle that's barely wider than a golf cart has genuine practical advantages.

Insurance & Registration: What You Need to Know

Importing a JDM car is one thing. Making it road-legal in Florida is another. Here's the quick version:

StepDetailsEstimated Cost
EPA & DOT complianceRequired at port of entry. Your broker handles this.$500–$2,000
Florida title & registrationVIN inspection at local tax collector's office, then standard registration.$300–$500
InsuranceSpecialty carriers like Hagerty, Grundy, or JC Taylor. Standard insurers often won't cover RHD vehicles.$1,200–$3,000/year
Headlight conversionJDM headlights aim left (for driving on the left). Many owners swap to USDM or aftermarket units.$200–$1,500

What's Next?

The JDM wave isn't slowing down. In 2027, we'll see 2002-model vehicles become legal, opening the door to the Nissan 350Z (JDM-spec), late-model Evos, and more S15 variants. Prices for the most desirable models — especially R34 GT-Rs and clean NSXs — are only going up as global demand outpaces supply.

If you've been thinking about getting into the JDM game, Miami is the place to do it. The infrastructure is here, the community is growing fast, and the cars have never been more accessible. Just don't sleep on it — the days of cheap Skylines are already behind us.

title: The Complete Guide to Tinting Your Car Windows in Miami: Laws, Shops & Best Films
excerpt: Window tint isn't optional in Miami — it's survival. Here's everything you need to know about Florida tint laws, the best shops in South Florida, and which films actually block the heat.
content:
If you've ever gotten into a car that's been sitting in a Miami parking lot at 2 PM in July, you understand why window tint isn't a cosmetic choice here — it's a necessity. The interior of an untinted car in direct Florida sun can reach 170°F. Your steering wheel becomes a branding iron. Your leather seats could fry an egg. And the UV exposure is silently destroying your dashboard, your skin, and your will to live.

This guide covers everything: Florida's tint laws (they're more lenient than you think), the different film technologies, the best shops in Miami, and what you should actually spend.

Florida Window Tint Laws (2026)

Florida Statute 316.2953 governs window tinting. Here's what's legal:

WindowSedansSUVs & VansNotes
WindshieldNon-reflective tint above AS-1 line onlyNon-reflective tint above AS-1 line onlyAS-1 line is top 5–6 inches
Front side windowsMust allow 28%+ light inMust allow 28%+ light in28% VLT minimum
Rear side windowsMust allow 15%+ light inAny darkness allowedSUVs get more freedom
Rear windowMust allow 15%+ light inAny darkness allowedSUVs/vans can go limo
ReflectivityMax 25% reflectiveMax 25% reflectiveNo mirror tint

Medical exemptions: Florida allows darker-than-legal tint with a medical exemption. A signed statement from a licensed physician citing a medical necessity (lupus, photosensitivity, melanoma history) must be kept in the vehicle. There's no specific VLT minimum with a medical exemption — but you'll need the paperwork if you get pulled over.

Tickets: A tint violation in Florida is a non-moving infraction. First offense is typically $116. Most officers won't pull you over solely for tint unless it's clearly limo-dark on the front windows. That said, it gives them a reason to stop you for something else. Stay at or above 28% on the front and you're fine.

Understanding Tint Film Technology

Not all tint is created equal. The difference between a $150 tint job and an $800 one is massive — and in Miami, it actually matters.

Film TypeHeat RejectionUV BlockDurabilityPrice (Full Car)Best For
Dyed filmLow (20–30%)Moderate2–5 years$150–$250Budget, cosmetic only
Metalized filmMedium (35–45%)Good5–8 years$250–$400Decent performance, may interfere with signals
Carbon filmGood (40–55%)Excellent8–12 years$350–$500Great value, no signal interference
Ceramic filmExcellent (50–70%)99%Lifetime$500–$900Best performance, worth it in Miami
IR ceramic (premium)Superior (60–85%)99%Lifetime$800–$1,500Maximum heat rejection, luxury vehicles

The bottom line: In Miami, ceramic is the move. The heat rejection difference between a $200 dyed film and a $600 ceramic film is the difference between your AC struggling at full blast and your car feeling comfortable within 30 seconds of starting it. Over a Florida summer, the fuel savings from reduced AC load alone can offset the price difference.

Top Window Tint Shops in Miami

We talked to local car communities, checked reviews, and visited shops to find the best tint installers in South Florida:

ShopLocationSpecialtyPrice Range (Full Car)Rating
Tint World (multiple)Kendall, Doral, Ft. LauderdaleNational chain, consistent quality, wide film selection$200–$8004.5/5
Xpel MiamiDoralPremium ceramic & PPF combo, OEM-level installs$600–$1,2004.8/5
305 Tint ShopHialeahHigh volume, fast turnaround, competitive pricing on ceramic$300–$7004.4/5
Elite Window FilmsCoral GablesLuxury vehicles, concours-quality installs, XPEL & 3M dealer$500–$1,5004.7/5
Sun StoppersAventuraLifetime warranty, good mid-range option, carbon & ceramic$350–$8004.5/5

What to Look For in a Quality Install

A bad tint job is worse than no tint at all. Here's how to tell the difference:

  • Single-piece rear window. Cheap shops cut the rear window film into strips. Quality shops heat-shrink a single piece to fit the curve. This is the #1 tell.
  • Clean edges. Film should be tucked under door seals, not cut short with visible gaps. No fingers, no bubbles, no debris trapped under the film.
  • Dot matrix coverage. The black dots around your windshield and rear glass (the frit band) are notoriously hard to adhere to. A good shop uses proper prep to prevent peeling in these areas.
  • Warranty. Ceramic films from reputable brands (XPEL, 3M, Llumar, SunTek) come with manufacturer lifetime warranties. If a shop won't warranty their work, walk away.
  • Cure time. Don't roll your windows down for 3–5 days after installation. Small water bubbles during the first week are normal — they'll evaporate. If they're still there after 2 weeks, go back.

Windshield Tint: The Game Changer

Florida law allows a non-reflective tint strip on the windshield above the AS-1 line (roughly the top 5 inches). But many Miami drivers go further with a full ceramic windshield film at 70% VLT — technically at the edge of legality, but the heat rejection benefits are enormous.

A ceramic windshield film at 70% VLT is nearly invisible but blocks up to 60% of infrared heat. The difference is immediately noticeable: your face and arms don't feel like they're under a heat lamp at red lights. Expect to pay $150–$300 for windshield ceramic tint alone.

Cost Breakdown: What to Budget

Vehicle TypeCarbon FilmCeramic FilmPremium Ceramic + Windshield
Sedan (4 windows + rear)$300–$450$500–$750$700–$1,000
SUV (6–8 windows + rear)$400–$550$600–$900$850–$1,200
Truck (crew cab)$350–$500$550–$800$750–$1,100
Exotic / sports car$450–$600$700–$1,100$1,000–$1,500

Final Verdict

If you're driving in Miami without quality window tint, you're suffering unnecessarily. Go ceramic — the upfront cost pays for itself in comfort, UV protection, and AC efficiency. Stay at 28% VLT or above on the front windows to stay legal, and find a shop that does single-piece rear windows with a lifetime warranty.

Your skin, your interior, and your electric bill will thank you.

title: Best Car Wrap Shops in Miami: Where to Transform Your Ride in 2026
excerpt: Miami is the undisputed car wrap capital of America. From chrome Lamborghinis on Collins Avenue to satin-black G-Wagons in Wynwood, wraps define the city's car scene. Here are the top shops doing the work.
content:
Walk down any block in South Beach, Brickell, or Wynwood and you'll see it: a matte purple Rolls-Royce parked next to a chrome-wrapped Ferrari next to a color-shifting Porsche that looks like it was dipped in liquid metal. Miami doesn't just embrace car wraps — it's the city that turned vinyl wrapping into an art form and a multi-million dollar industry.

The numbers back it up. South Florida has more vehicle wrap shops per capita than any other metro in the United States, and the demand shows no signs of slowing. Between Miami's year-round sun (which punishes factory paint), its status as a supercar capital, and a culture that rewards visual boldness, wrapping your car here isn't vanity — it's almost practical.

Why Wraps Dominate in Miami

Factory paint in Miami takes a beating. The UV index regularly hits extreme levels, salt air corrodes clear coats, and the occasional hurricane-season debris doesn't help. A quality vinyl wrap serves as armor for your original paint while letting you change your car's entire personality — and when you sell or return a lease, you peel it off and the factory finish underneath is pristine.

For the exotic car crowd, wraps also solve a practical problem: when you're leasing a 00,000 Lamborghini Huracán, you can't exactly repaint it. But a ,000 wrap? That's reversible, Instagram-ready, and turns heads at every valet stand on Ocean Drive.

What Car Wraps Actually Cost in Miami

Wrap TypePrice RangeLifespanBest For
Full Color Change (Sedan),000 – ,0003–5 yearsDaily drivers wanting a new look
Full Color Change (SUV/Truck),500 – ,0003–5 yearsG-Wagons, Urus, Escalade
Full Color Change (Exotic),000 – 0,000+3–5 yearsFerraris, Lambos, McLarens
Chrome / Mirror Finish,000 – 2,0002–3 yearsMaximum attention (South Beach specials)
Satin / Matte Finish,500 – ,5003–5 yearsUnderstated luxury (Brickell crowd)
Partial Wrap (Accents/Stripes)00 – ,0003–5 yearsRacing stripes, roof wraps, mirror caps
Paint Protection Film (PPF),500 – ,0005–10 yearsClear protection from rock chips and UV

Prices vary based on vehicle complexity, film quality (3M, Avery Dennison, and XPEL are the big three), and shop reputation. The cheapest quote isn't always the best — a poorly applied wrap bubbles, peels, and can actually damage your paint on removal.

Top Car Wrap Shops in Miami

1. MetroWrapz (Opa-locka)

The name most associated with Miami wraps. MetroWrapz has built a national reputation wrapping cars for athletes, rappers, and influencers, but they also handle everyday vehicles. Their Opa-locka facility is massive, and their Instagram feed is essentially a rolling showcase of Miami car culture. Known for: color-shifting wraps, celebrity builds, and chrome finishes that shouldn't work but somehow do.

2. Wrapped Studios (Miami)

A newer shop that's earned a loyal following for clean, precise installations. They specialize in satin and matte finishes — the kind of understated work that Brickell Porsche owners love. Their PPF + wrap combo packages are competitively priced, and their attention to panel alignment and edge tucking is exceptional.

3. WrapBullys (Hialeah)

If you want something wild — color-shifting Lamborghinis, holographic Challengers, or neon-accented exotics — WrapBullys is where Miami's flashiest builds happen. Based in Hialeah, they've become a go-to for the South Florida car scene's most over-the-top transformations. Not for the subtle, but absolutely for the unforgettable.

4. Xclusive Wraps (Doral)

A shop that's carved out a niche in the commercial space while still doing high-end personal vehicles. Their fleet wrap work for Miami businesses is top-tier, and they bring that same precision to color changes on everything from Tesla Model 3s to Bentley Continentals. Good value for the quality.

5. SunTek Miami / XPEL Miami Certified Shops

If your priority is paint protection rather than color change, look for certified XPEL or SunTek installers. These shops specialize in PPF — the clear, self-healing film that protects against rock chips, bug acid, and Miami's brutal UV exposure. Several Miami dealers now pre-install PPF on new exotics before delivery.

What to Ask Before You Wrap

Not all wrap shops are equal, and Miami has enough fly-by-night installers to make due diligence essential. Before committing:

• What film brand do they use? 3M 2080, Avery Dennison Supreme, and XPEL are industry standards. Off-brand films save money upfront but fail faster.
• Do they remove bumpers, mirrors, and door handles? A quality shop disassembles panels for clean edges. A cheap shop wraps around them and you'll see seams everywhere.
• What's the warranty? Reputable shops offer 1–3 year installation warranties on top of manufacturer film warranties.
• Can you see their portfolio? Any shop worth visiting has hundreds of photos of completed work. Look for consistency and clean edges, not just flashy colors.
• How long will it take? A proper full wrap takes 3–5 days. Anyone promising overnight is cutting corners.

Wrap Trends Dominating Miami in 2026

Satin everything. Satin black, satin military green, satin cement gray — the matte-adjacent finish has overtaken gloss as the most requested color change in Miami shops. It reads expensive without screaming for attention.

Color-shifting and iridescent films. The opposite of satin's restraint. These films change color depending on the angle and light, and they're all over Miami's exotic car scene. Think purple-to-teal or bronze-to-green shifts that look different in every Instagram photo.

Two-tone combos. Black roof and pillars with a contrasting body color — a factory option on some cars that wrap shops can apply to any vehicle. Particularly popular on SUVs and sedans.

PPF + ceramic coating combos. The practical crowd is layering paint protection film with ceramic coating for maximum durability. It's not cheap (,000–2,000 for a full vehicle), but in Miami's environment, the protection is worth it for any car you plan to keep.

Will a Wrap Affect Resale Value?

If done properly, a wrap actually protects resale value by preserving the factory paint underneath. When you remove a professionally installed wrap, the paint should be in better condition than an unwrapped car that spent years in Miami sun and salt air.

The key word is professionally. A cheap wrap that's been on too long, applied over damaged paint, or removed incorrectly can leave adhesive residue or pull clear coat. This is why shop selection matters more than price.

For leased vehicles — which make up a huge portion of Miami's exotic fleet — wraps are essentially mandatory customization. They let you personalize without violating lease terms, and removal before return is straightforward.

The Bottom Line

Miami's wrap scene is the best in the country, and it's not close. Whether you want to protect a new Ferrari's paint with invisible PPF or turn your Model Y into a rolling work of art, the talent and technology here is world-class. Just do your homework, choose a reputable shop, and budget for quality — your car (and your Instagram feed) will thank you.

title: 5 Best Night Drives in Miami Every Car Enthusiast Should Experience
excerpt: Miami transforms after dark — the neon glow, empty causeways, and ocean breeze make it one of the best cities in America for a late-night cruise. Here are five routes worth staying up for.
content:
There's a version of Miami that only exists after 10 PM. The traffic thins out, the skyline lights up, and the causeways open up into long, sweeping stretches of asphalt with nothing but water on both sides and a warm breeze through the window. For car enthusiasts, nighttime Miami is an entirely different driving experience — one that transforms ordinary commuter routes into cinematic cruises.

Whether you're in a drop-top exotic, a built Honda Civic, or just your daily driver with the windows down, these five routes deliver the best of Miami after dark.

1. The Rickenbacker Causeway Loop

Route: Brickell → Rickenbacker Causeway → Key Biscayne → loop back
Distance: ~14 miles round trip
Best time: 10 PM – midnight
Vibe: Open water, city skyline views, quiet curves

This is the definitive Miami night drive. The Rickenbacker Causeway rises over Biscayne Bay with the downtown skyline glittering to your left and the dark Atlantic stretching to your right. The toll plaza is empty late at night, the bridge's sweeping arc feels like a runway, and once you're on Key Biscayne, Crandon Boulevard winds through canopied trees with almost zero traffic.

The turnaround at Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park puts you at the southernmost point of the barrier island. On the return trip, the view of downtown Miami's skyline reflected in the bay is genuinely breathtaking. Roll the windows down, keep it under the limit, and just absorb it.

Pro tip: Stop at the top of the Rickenbacker Bridge on the return. The pull-off area (technically for fishermen) offers one of the best skyline photo ops in Miami — and it's almost empty after dark.

2. Collins Avenue: South Beach to Bal Harbour

Route: South Pointe → Collins Avenue north → Bal Harbour Shops
Distance: ~10 miles one way
Best time: 11 PM – 1 AM (after the dinner crowd, before the club exodus)
Vibe: Neon Art Deco, people-watching at stoplights, cruise control

Collins Avenue at night is Miami distilled into a single road. Starting from South Pointe, you crawl past the Art Deco hotels of South Beach — their neon facades reflecting off your hood — through the mid-Beach hotels, past the Fontainebleau and Eden Roc, and up into the quieter, tree-lined stretch of Surfside and Bal Harbour.

This isn't a speed run. Collins is about being seen as much as seeing. The stoplights are frequent, which is actually perfect — each red light is a chance to look around at the automotive circus that is South Beach at night. You'll spot Rolls-Royces with starlight headliners, wrapped Lamborghinis with LED underbody kits, and vintage convertibles that look like they rolled off a movie set.

Pro tip: Start at Joe's Stone Crab end of South Beach and work north. The southbound return on Indian Creek Drive is quieter and residential — a nice contrast to Collins's energy.

3. Brickell to Coconut Grove via South Bayshore Drive

Route: Brickell Avenue south → South Miami Avenue → South Bayshore Drive → Coconut Grove
Distance: ~6 miles one way
Best time: 9 PM – 11 PM
Vibe: Waterfront canopy, old Miami money, banyan tree tunnels

This short route packs more visual texture per mile than almost anything else in Miami. You start in Brickell's glass-and-steel canyon, pass through the developing Underline park corridor, and then suddenly you're on South Bayshore Drive — a winding waterfront road lined with massive banyan trees that form a natural tunnel overhead.

At night, the banyans are lit by ambient light from the waterfront estates, creating an almost gothic atmosphere that feels nothing like the rest of Miami. The road curves along the bay with Biscayne Bay visible through the trees, and you end up in Coconut Grove's village center, which has its own laid-back nightlife energy.

Pro tip: Continue south on Main Highway past the Barnacle Historic State Park for an even quieter, more atmospheric stretch. The road narrows and the canopy thickens — it feels like driving through a tunnel of green, even at night.

4. The MacArthur Causeway to the Port of Miami Loop

Route: Downtown Miami → MacArthur Causeway → Star Island → Palm Island → Port of Miami loop
Distance: ~8 miles with detours
Best time: Midnight – 2 AM
Vibe: Urban skyline, cruise ship row, island wealth on display

The MacArthur Causeway is the I-395 bridge that connects downtown to South Beach, but at night it becomes something else entirely. The view from the causeway encompasses the entire Miami skyline on one side and the cruise ships docked at PortMiami on the other — those massive vessels lit up like floating cities are an unexpectedly dramatic backdrop for a night cruise.

The detour is what makes this route special. Exit onto Star Island or Palm Island (public roads, despite the guard gates — just tell them you're sightseeing) and loop past some of the most expensive real estate in America. At night, the waterfront mansions are lit up and the streets are dead quiet. It's surreal driving a 25 mph loop past 0 million homes with the downtown skyline as your backdrop.

Pro tip: Time this for when a cruise ship is departing (usually around 4–5 PM for the best light, but late-night Saturday departures happen too). A lit-up cruise ship pulling away from port while you're on the causeway is a genuinely cinematic moment.

5. US-1 South: Cutler Bay to Key Largo

Route: Florida City → US-1 south → Key Largo (Mile Marker 106)
Distance: ~30 miles one way
Best time: 10 PM – midnight (weeknights especially)
Vibe: Open road, mangrove darkness, bridge running lights, escapism

This is the drive for when you need to go. Heading south out of Florida City, US-1 enters the 18-mile stretch through the mangroves that connects the mainland to the Keys. At night, it's pitch black on both sides — just your headlights, the road, and the occasional reflective eyes of a Key deer or raccoon on the shoulder.

When you hit Key Largo, the road narrows and you're surrounded by water. Card Sound Road (the alternate route) is even more atmospheric — a two-lane road through total darkness with a vintage toll bridge that feels like crossing into another world.

This isn't a flashy Miami cruise. This is the antidote to Miami — raw, quiet, and slightly wild. Turn the music off for a stretch and just listen to the wind and the occasional splash of something large in the mangroves. Then turn around and watch Miami's glow appear on the horizon as you drive back north.

Pro tip: Stop at Alabama Jack's in Card Sound (if they're still open when you pass) for waterfront drinks in a setting that feels like it's 100 years and 100 miles from South Beach. It's neither — it's 45 minutes away.

Night Driving Tips for Miami

• Watch for speed traps. Miami Beach PD and Coral Gables PD are especially active late at night on causeways and main drags. Keep it legal — the routes are better at cruise speed anyway.
• DUI checkpoints are common on Friday and Saturday nights, especially on the causeways and US-1. Miami-Dade Police doesn't announce them in advance.
• Wildlife on US-1. South of Florida City, deer, iguanas, and raccoons cross the road regularly at night. Stay alert.
• Toll roads. The Rickenbacker Causeway has a toll (.25 with SunPass). The causeways and expressways are mostly cashless — make sure you have SunPass or Toll-by-Plate set up.
• Convertible weather. March through May is peak drop-top season — low humidity, warm nights, no mosquitoes. Take advantage.

The Bottom Line

Miami's daytime driving is a battle — traffic, construction, aggressive mergers on the Palmetto. But the same city at night becomes one of the most rewarding places to drive in America. The skyline, the water, the warm air, the neon — it all comes together after dark in a way that makes you remember why you love cars in the first place. Pick a route, pick a playlist, and go.

title: How to Ship a Car to Miami: Complete Guide for 2026
excerpt: Moving to Miami or buying a car out of state? Here's everything you need to know about shipping a vehicle to South Florida — costs, timelines, carriers, and the mistakes that cost people thousands.
content:
Miami is the number one destination for vehicle shipments in the southeastern United States — and it's not close. Between the steady stream of people relocating from the Northeast, snowbirds shuttling cars between seasonal homes, out-of-state exotic car purchases, and the booming used luxury market, auto transport carriers run routes to South Florida more frequently than almost any other corridor in the country.

That demand means competitive pricing, but it also means a crowded market full of brokers, middlemen, and operators of wildly varying quality. Here's how to ship a car to Miami without overpaying, getting scammed, or having your vehicle arrive with new damage.

Open vs. Enclosed Transport

The first decision is how exposed you want your car to be during transit.

Transport TypeCost (to Miami)Best ForRisks
Open Carrier00 – ,500Standard vehicles, daily drivers, newer cars under 0KExposed to weather, road debris, dust. Cosmetic risk is real but minor damage is uncommon.
Enclosed Carrier,400 – ,000+Exotics, classics, high-value vehicles, anything over 5KMinimal. Fully protected from elements. Fewer carriers available, so booking windows are longer.
Single-Car Enclosed,500 – ,000+Ultra-high-value cars, concours vehicles, one-of-a-kind buildsWhite-glove service. Expensive but the car gets individual attention.

For most people moving a normal car to Miami, open transport is perfectly fine. Your vehicle shares a carrier with 7–10 other cars, and while it's exposed to the elements, actual transit damage from open carriers is statistically rare — well under 1% of shipments.

If you're shipping anything exotic, classic, or worth more than 5,000, enclosed is worth the premium. Miami's luxury car market means enclosed carriers run the I-95 corridor constantly, so availability is better here than in most markets.

What It Costs to Ship a Car to Miami

OriginOpen CarrierEnclosed CarrierTransit Time
New York / New Jersey00 – ,300,500 – ,5003–5 days
Boston / New England,000 – ,400,600 – ,8004–6 days
Chicago / Midwest,000 – ,500,700 – ,8004–7 days
Los Angeles / West Coast,200 – ,800,000 – ,5007–10 days
Dallas / Houston00 – ,200,400 – ,2003–5 days
Atlanta / Southeast00 – 00,000 – ,8002–3 days

Prices fluctuate seasonally. October through December (snowbird migration south) and March through May (snowbird migration north) are peak season on the Miami corridor, and prices can jump 20–30%. If you have flexibility, shipping in the off-peak summer months saves real money.

How to Choose a Car Shipping Company

The auto transport industry has a reputation problem — and it's partly deserved. The market is dominated by brokers who take your booking, then farm it out to independent carriers. The broker model isn't inherently bad (brokers can access a wider network of carriers), but it means the company you pay isn't always the company that shows up with your car.

Here's how to navigate it:

Check FMCSA registration. Every legitimate auto transport company must be registered with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. Search their MC number at safer.fmcsa.dot.gov to verify they're licensed and insured.

Read reviews — but read them right. Google Reviews and Transport Reviews are the most reliable. Be skeptical of companies with only 5-star reviews (likely filtered or incentivized). Look for patterns in complaints: repeated mentions of late delivery, damage, or surprise fees are red flags.

Get the insurance details in writing. Ask for a copy of the carrier's cargo insurance certificate before your car gets loaded. Standard coverage is 00,000–50,000 per carrier load, but know the deductible and claims process. Your own auto insurance or credit card may provide additional coverage.

Avoid massive upfront deposits. A reasonable deposit is 00–00 to book. Any company demanding full payment before pickup is a risk. Pay the balance to the driver on delivery (industry standard).

Get everything in writing. The Bill of Lading (BOL) is your contract. It documents the vehicle condition at pickup and delivery. Inspect your car thoroughly at both ends and note any damage on the BOL before signing.

Recommended Companies for Miami Shipments

These carriers and brokers have strong reputations on the South Florida corridor:

• Montway Auto Transport — One of the largest brokers in the US. Competitive pricing, good tracking, and consistent service on the I-95 corridor to Miami.
• Sherpa Auto Transport — Known for a price-lock guarantee (the quote is the price, period). Slightly higher than average but no surprise fees.
• Enclosed Auto Transport (EAT) — Specialist in enclosed shipments. If you're shipping a six-figure exotic to Miami, they run the East Coast corridor weekly.
• AmeriFreight — Budget-friendly broker with consistently good reviews. Good for standard vehicles where you want to minimize cost.
• Guardian Auto Transport — Strong Miami presence with terminal options in Doral for local pickup. Good for snowbirds who need seasonal round-trip service.

Preparing Your Car for Shipping

A few steps before pickup protect your vehicle and speed up the process:

• Wash the car. A clean vehicle makes it easier to document pre-existing damage during the pickup inspection.
• Remove personal items. Carriers aren't insured for personal belongings inside the vehicle. Remove electronics, loose items, and anything valuable. Most carriers allow up to 100 lbs of items in the trunk, but they won't cover loss or damage.
• Document everything. Take dated photos and video of all four sides, the roof, interior, odometer, and any existing damage before the carrier arrives.
• Leave about 1/4 tank of gas. Enough for the carrier to load/unload and for you to drive to a station on delivery. A full tank adds weight and cost.
• Disable toll transponders. Remove or deactivate your SunPass, E-ZPass, or toll tag so you don't get charged for the carrier's route.
• Provide keys and instructions. If the car has a valet mode, alarm kill switch, or any quirks, let the driver know.

After Your Car Arrives in Miami: Registration and Insurance

If you're relocating permanently, Florida requires you to register your vehicle and obtain a Florida driver's license within 30 days of establishing residency. Here's the quick version:

StepWhereCostNotes
Get Florida auto insuranceAny insurerVaries (Miami is expensive)Must have PIP + property damage liability minimum
Get a VIN inspectionAny FL tax collector officesh (included in registration)Required for out-of-state vehicles
Register the vehicleMiami-Dade Tax Collector25 – 50+ (depends on weight)Bring title, out-of-state registration, proof of insurance, FL driver's license
Get a Florida driver's licenseFLHSMV office8Surrender your out-of-state license

Important: Florida has no state income tax, but it makes up for it with higher registration fees and insurance costs. Miami-Dade has some of the highest auto insurance premiums in the country — budget 00–00/month for a standard vehicle and significantly more for exotics. Shop aggressively and consider bundling home + auto if you're also buying property.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Booking the cheapest quote. The lowest price in auto transport often means the longest wait. Carriers pick loads that pay the best, and a below-market quote may sit unassigned for weeks. A fair-market quote gets your car moving faster.

Not inspecting at delivery. The Bill of Lading protects you — but only if you document damage at the time of delivery. Inspect the vehicle thoroughly in good lighting before signing the BOL as received. Once you sign, proving transit damage gets exponentially harder.

Ignoring the 30-day registration window. Florida police do enforce the 30-day registration requirement, especially in Miami-Dade. Driving on out-of-state plates months after moving is a ticketable offense, and your out-of-state insurance may not cover a Florida accident properly.

Forgetting about Florida's title requirements. If you have a lien on your vehicle, your lender needs to send the title to Florida. This can take weeks. Start the process before your car arrives.

The Bottom Line

Shipping a car to Miami is straightforward if you do your homework. The I-95 corridor is one of the most-traveled auto transport routes in the country, which means competitive pricing and frequent availability. Choose a reputable company, document everything, and budget a few hundred extra for Florida's registration and insurance requirements on the other end. Your car will be sitting in Miami sunshine before you know it.
